summary: Develops an architecture and set of requirements for alerting dormant mobile hosts, commonly called paging. It guides development of an IP protocol for the task.

plainLanguage.summary: It sketches how to gently wake up a sleeping phone when someone needs it.

questions: what is a dormant mode host
subtitle: Requirements and architecture for waking dormant mobile IP hosts when they receive packets.

tldr.problem: Mobile hosts save power by entering dormant mode, but then cannot receive packets. Someone needs to wake them up when data arrives, but doing this at IP layer has never been formally specified.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a functional architecture with five entities: Hosts in dormant or inactive mode, Paging Agents that alert the host, Tracking Agents that track host location, Dormant Monitoring Agents that detect incoming packets, and interfaces between them.
tldr.outcome: This architecture and 27 requirements guide the development of an IP paging protocol to efficiently wake sleeping hosts without excessive power drain or security vulnerabilities.

today: RFC 3154 is an Informational RFC that provides the foundational architecture and requirements for IP paging. While it is not a protocol standard itself, it guided development of paging protocols and remains relevant for implementations of host alerting in mobile IP networks.

sections.title: Problem and Motivation
sections.content:
Mobile hosts like cell phones and laptops need to conserve power. One way is to enter dormant mode, where they stop listening for packets and turn off radios. However, while dormant, they cannot receive incoming data. The network somehow needs to alert them when a packet arrives.

Currently, some wireless networks handle this at Layer 2 (the radio protocol level). However, the Internet Protocol layer has no standard way to do this. As IP networks expand to cover wireless devices, and as mobile IP becomes more common, an IP-level paging protocol becomes necessary.

This RFC develops an architecture and requirements to guide creation of such a protocol. It is not itself a protocol specification, but rather a requirements and architecture document.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones turn off their radios to save batteries, but then they can't hear when someone calls. This explains how IP networks can tap the phone to wake it up.

sections.title: Security Threats and Requirements
sections.content:
An IP paging protocol introduces several security challenges not present in traditional network protocols:

DoS Amplification: An attacker can send bogus packets claiming to be from different senders, destined for hosts in dormant mode. The paging system broadcasts wake-up messages, amplifying the attack across entire networks. Wireless networks are especially vulnerable due to scarce bandwidth. Additionally, an attacker might target a host that declares itself dormant but never responds to pages, creating a vector for indefinite amplification.

Queue Overflow: If the network buffers incoming packets while a host is dormant (for reliability), an attacker can flood the queue with bogus packets destined for many hosts. When the dormant hosts don't respond, the queue overflows and legitimate packets are dropped.

Selective DoS Against Hosts: By sending frequent packets, an attacker can prevent a host from entering dormant mode, draining its battery. Bogus paging area information can confuse hosts about their location. Fake paging messages from bogus agents can cause similar problems.

The RFC specifies 27 requirements, including strict authentication of paging messages, location registrations, and paging area information; secure handling of dormant mode state; and methods to detect and reject bogus senders before paging messages are sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad people could trick the network into repeatedly waking a phone (wasting battery), filling up the wake-up queue, or sending fake wake-up calls. The protocol needs ways to prove messages are real and to stop attacks.

sections.title: Functional Architecture and Entities
sections.content:
Host (H): An IP host that can enter dormant mode to conserve power. It supports some protocol (possibly proprietary L2 or time-slotted wake-up) to receive paging alerts. The host tracks which paging area it is in and informs the Tracking Agent when the area changes.

Paging Agent (PA): Responsible for alerting hosts when packets arrive. It periodically broadcasts information identifying the paging area. Alert mechanism depends on L2 and the host's dormant mode implementation.

Tracking Agent (TA): Tracks the host's location (which paging area) while dormant or active. It receives location updates from the host when the host changes paging area. There is a one-to-one mapping between host and tracking agent. It reports the correct paging agent to contact when a packet arrives.

Dormant Monitoring Agent (DMA): Detects when packets arrive for hosts with no active route (hosts in dormant mode). It queries the Tracking Agent to find the correct Paging Agent, then instructs that agent to page the host. Once the host becomes routable, the DMA arranges packet delivery.

These five functional entities communicate through five defined interfaces: H-PA (paging area broadcasts, page alerts), H-TA (location updates, dormant mode notifications), H-DMA (registration with filtering information), DMA-TA (packet arrival reports, paging agent lookup), and DMA-PA (page requests, page responses).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of five helpers: the phone (host) tells a tracker where it is; a pager waits to hear from the network; a monitoring agent notices when mail arrives; and they talk to each other through five different channels to wake the phone when needed.

sections.title: Key Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies 27 numbered requirements across several categories:

Performance: Protocol MUST minimize impact on power consumption (the whole point of dormant mode). It MUST scale to millions of hosts. It SHOULD provide mechanisms to determine whether a host is completely inactive (out of range) to avoid wasteful paging.

Flexibility: MUST work with different dormant mode implementations. MUST be independent of any specific mobility protocol, though it SHOULD support mobile IPv4 and IPv6. MUST allow arbitrary mapping between subnets and paging areas. SHOULD support multiple dormant modes simultaneously.

Robustness: MUST be robust against network element failures and message loss. SHOULD provide filtering mechanisms so hosts only wake for relevant broadcast/multicast/anycast traffic. MUST provide reliable packet delivery to high probability.

Security (detailed above): MUST authenticate location registrations, paging area information, and paging messages. MUST detect bogus correspondent nodes. Security mechanisms SHOULD NOT require power consumption while dormant. MUST NOT interfere with host security policy or end-to-end security.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol needs to: use little power, work with millions of phones, handle all types of sleep modes, survive lost messages and broken network parts, and defend against attacks.

sections.title: Framework and Future Development
sections.content:
This RFC provides a framework for protocol development, not a complete protocol. It separates logical functional entities from physical implementation, meaning a physical device can combine multiple entities.

The architecture makes no assumptions about whether L2 (wireless link layer) paging is available, allowing protocols to be designed that work with or without it. The requirement that protocols support both mobile IPv4 and IPv6, and work without any mobility protocol, ensures broad applicability.

Implementation of the five defined interfaces is where protocol development occurs. Not all interfaces necessarily require new protocols; if functional entities are combined in a single device, some interfaces may use internal APIs rather than network protocols.

The security section identifies threats unique to paging that must be addressed. The architecture guides developers to think about all five functional entities, even if they design a system that merges several into single network elements, ensuring nothing is overlooked.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a blueprint, not a finished protocol. It shows what parts need to talk to each other and what they need to do, and lets implementers decide how to build it.
